name: Skin
summary: Skin is the body's largest barrier. Its outer layer, the epidermis, is built of keratinocytes that flatten and die into a tough surface coat; Langerhans cells and memory T cells live among them. The dermis below holds blood capillaries, lymph vessels and resident macrophages, mast cells and dendritic cells. This view shows a fresh cut, drawn roughly to scale and about a quarter of a millimetre across: platelets plug it while the first white cells arrive. Pick a cell.

residents.note: Sits among the keratinocytes of the epidermis, reaching long arms between them, even through the tight junctions under the dead surface layer, to sample what gets in (shown in mice). Carrying what it has picked up, it can travel through lymph vessels to the nearest lymph node. In healthy human skin it activates regulatory T cells to keep the peace, and with a pathogen present it activates resident memory T cells instead. Whether it mainly starts or restrains immune responses is debated.

Skin holds about 2 × 10¹⁰ T cells, nearly twice the number in the blood, and many are memory cells. Resident memory T cells stay after an infection has cleared, many of them CD8 cells in the epidermis in mice and, in people, mostly CD4 cells in the dermis, ready to respond at once if the same microbe comes back and to sound an alarm in the tissue around them. Other memory cells recirculate between skin, lymph and blood.
Platelets leaking from cut vessels stick to the exposed collagen, clump together and, with fibrin, plug the wound within minutes. They also release signals that call in white cells.
Absent from healthy skin. Within hours of a cut, neutrophils leave the blood through small venules near the wound and crawl toward it, where they swallow and kill bacteria.
Th17 cells in the skin make IL-17 and IL-22, which call in neutrophils and make keratinocytes produce antimicrobial proteins.
Leaves the blood after the first neutrophils and turns into macrophages that clear the debris and help the wound heal.
Dermal macrophages stay put, swallowing microbes and debris that get through and sending signals that call in neutrophils.

Sits beside small blood vessels in the dermis. Injury, microbes or allergen meeting the IgE on its surface make it release histamine and TNF within minutes: nearby vessels leak, neutrophils are called in and dendritic cells leave for the lymph node sooner (the last shown in mice). Regulatory T cells can block its release, and in mouse dermis neighbouring innate lymphoid cells damp it with IL-13.
Dermal dendritic cells pick up antigen in the dermis, then squeeze into lymph vessels and travel to the nearest lymph node to show it to T cells.
Absent from healthy skin, but flows into fresh wounds and makes type I interferons that help the skin heal (seen in mouse and human wounds).

Healthy human skin holds a few innate lymphoid cells, mainly groups 2 and 3. Without recognising any antigen, they react to alarm signals from skin cells: ILC2 make IL-13 and IL-5 (in mouse dermis, beside mast cells) and ILC3 make IL-22 and IL-17. Their numbers rise in some skin diseases, including atopic dermatitis and psoriasis.
